content:
Late Princess Diana's youngest brother Charles Spencer has alleged in a new book that Prince Charles (now King) claimed the public would quickly forget her after her tragic death in 1997. The claims come from Spencer's upcoming memoir.

According to excerpts from the new book "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" published by the Daily Mail on Wednesday, Spencer claimed he had a heated phone argument with the now-King over whether William and Harry should appear in the funeral procession for their mother.

In the book, to be published next week, Spencer wrote: "Prince Charles continued to vent his anger, and I let him speak without interruption, then he stopped."

Spencer quoted the other party as saying: "I thought he paused to calm down, but then he erupted down the phone. I have always believed it was his long-suppressed contempt for Diana, and his fear that the whole world was shocked by her death. 'Don't worry,' he said through gritted teeth, 'they will forget her soon enough!'"

Spencer wrote that he was left "stunned" by the remarks and needed a few seconds to react.

He wrote: "I said very calmly: 'I really cannot believe you would say such a thing.' Then I hung up."

The Daily Mail reported on Tuesday that four copies of Spencer's book were stolen by thieves from a van in the Netherlands, and Dutch authorities are investigating the burglary.

A publishing source described the theft as "extremely suspicious", telling the Daily Mail: "Nothing like this has ever happened before."

They told the Daily Mail: "This may be the most important book of the year, and security for it has been extremely tight."

Spencer's representatives did not immediately respond to HuffPost's request for comment.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson issued a statement in response to HuffPost's inquiry: "While we would not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty understands that the grief of losing a sibling can sometimes cause people to lose their senses, affect their judgment, and distort their memories, even after many years, in ways that others may not perceive."

Spencer delivered a moving eulogy at Diana's funeral at Westminster Abbey, criticising the British tabloids for their intrusive pursuit of information, describing his sister as "the most hunted figure of the modern age."

Spencer previously posted on social media that the new book was "the most personally emotional of the ten books I have written over the past thirty years."

He wrote: "Ultimately, this is a younger brother's simplest salute to an extraordinary sister."

Carly Ledbetter contributed to this report.
